incidents.title: Unbounded in-memory queue
incidents.brief: Producers keep appending jobs in RAM while workers are stuck, and the process OOMs.
incidents.constraint: Work arrives faster than it completes.
incidents.question: What should producers see?

choices.label: Bound queue
choices.resultBody: A bounded queue that blocks, drops, or returns 429 when full instead of growing forever.

choices.label: Infinite buffer
choices.resultBody: An infinite buffer absorbs 4,000 jobs/s while workers are stuck, so memory climbs until the process is killed and every queued job in RAM is lost.

choices.label: Ignore lag
choices.resultBody: Ignoring worker lag lets the queue grow silently; by the time anyone looks, jobs are 50 minutes stale and the process runs out of memory anyway.

hints: Work arrives faster than it completes.
Unbounded buffers hide the fire.
Slow or reject producers.

incidents.title: Uploads say done, videos appear 6 hours later
incidents.brief: Clipstream's upload API returns 200 for every video. 7,200 uploads/min arrive, transcoders clear 5,000/min, and the queue holds 1.8 million jobs: a 6-hour wait users never see.
incidents.constraint: Transcode capacity is fixed until next quarter's GPU order.
incidents.question: What should the API tell uploaders once the backlog is too deep?

choices.label: Cap the queue and return 503 with Retry-After

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Honest, bounded wait; about 30% of peak uploads are deferred to off-peak.

choices.resultBody: The queue is capped at 150,000 jobs (~30 min of work); accepted uploads get 202 with a status URL, and the rest get 503 with Retry-After: 120, which the client retries with jitter. Cost: at peak ~30% of uploads are deferred, and clients must implement the retry.

choices.label: Autoscale the upload API to accept more videos
choices.resultBody: The API was never the bottleneck: with transcoders fixed at 5,000 jobs/min and 7,200 arriving, the queue still grows by 2,200 a minute and the wait passes 6.3 hours.

choices.label: Show a progress bar and hide queue depth
choices.resultBody: The bar stalls at 99%, users assume failure and upload again, and the duplicates push the backlog to 2.1 million jobs while tickets double to 260 an hour.

hints: The transcoders are doing their best; the promise at the front door is wrong.
An unbounded backlog turns a fast failure into a slow, invisible one.
HTTP status codes can carry a 'come back later' time.

incidents.title: Order-events consumer blows its heap every 12 minutes
incidents.brief: Shipwise's reactive consumer fetches 20,000 records/s from Kafka into memory, but its enrichment step can only do 500/s. The in-memory buffer passes 6 GB and the JVM OOMs every 12 minutes.
incidents.constraint: Enrichment calls a partner API hard-capped at 500 req/s across all consumers.
incidents.question: How should the consumer signal how much it can take?

choices.label: Pause partitions when in-flight records exceed 2,000

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Memory bounded; the backlog moves into Kafka as consumer lag.

choices.resultBody: The consumer calls pause() at 2,000 in-flight records and resume() below 500, still polling so it keeps its group membership; fetches match the 500/s partner cap and heap settles at 700 MB. Cost: the backlog now shows up as consumer lag, so topic retention must cover it and lag alerts replace OOM alerts.

choices.label: Raise the consumer heap from 8 GB to 32 GB
choices.resultBody: The buffer still grows by 19,500 records/s, so 32 GB only delays the crash, and multi-second full-GC pauses now trigger consumer-group rebalances on top.

choices.label: Add partitions and scale out to 40 consumer pods
choices.resultBody: 40 pods fetch in parallel, but the partner cap is still 500 req/s in total; each pod buffers its share, the partner starts returning 429s, and the pods' retries push errors to 900/s.

hints: Kafka is pull-based: who decides how much gets pulled?
The slow step's rate is fixed, so the buffer in front of it must be bounded.
The consumer API can stop fetching from partitions without leaving the group.

incidents.title: gRPC stream server fills its heap with unsent frames
incidents.brief: Tracefeed streams 40 MB/s of telemetry per client over gRPC. Slow mobile dashboards drain 2 MB/s, yet the server keeps calling onNext(), and 3 GB of queued frames pile up in memory.
incidents.constraint: HTTP/2 already enforces per-stream flow-control windows between client and server.
incidents.question: How should the server react to a slow reader?

choices.label: Send only when isReady(), resume in the onReady handler

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Memory bounded by the window; slow clients must receive sampled data.

choices.resultBody: The server checks isReady() before each onNext() and parks the stream until the onReady handler fires, so writes follow the client's HTTP/2 window and queued frames drop to 40 MB. Cost: a 2 MB/s client can't get 40 MB/s, so the server now samples or drops stale telemetry for slow streams.

choices.label: Raise the HTTP/2 stream window to 64 MB
choices.resultBody: A larger window lets the server push more before blocking, but the phone still reads 2 MB/s; buffers swell on both ends and delay grows to 60 s.

choices.label: Spill each stream's pending frames to local disk
choices.resultBody: The heap OOM turns into ~130 GB/hour of disk writes; dashboards fall 10 minutes behind live data and the volume fills before the evening peak.

hints: The protocol is already saying 'slow down'; the application isn't listening.
Flow-control windows only help if the sender waits when they close.
Look at the stream observer's readiness signal.

incidents.title: Checkout times out behind bulk CSV exports
incidents.brief: At 11:00 Tallybook's API receives 14,000 req/s against 9,000 req/s of capacity. Checkout, bulk CSV exports and health checks share one queue, and every class times out after 30 s.
incidents.constraint: Checkout revenue must be protected; exports can wait several minutes.
incidents.question: Which requests should fail first, and where?

choices.label: Shed exports first via priority admission at the gateway

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Critical traffic protected; low-priority work is deferred and the priority map needs upkeep.

choices.resultBody: The gateway tags requests critical, default or sheddable; above the concurrency limit it rejects exports with 503 + Retry-After before they use any API capacity, and checkout p95 returns to 180 ms. Cost: exports stall for ~20 minutes at peak, and the priority map must be kept current as endpoints change.

choices.label: Lower every request timeout from 30 s to 5 s
choices.resultBody: Requests now die at 5 s instead of 30 s, but checkout still waits in the same queue behind exports, so about a third of checkouts keep timing out.

choices.label: Randomly drop 35% of requests at the load balancer
choices.resultBody: Random drop brings load under 9,000 req/s, but it rejects checkouts as readily as exports: 35% of paying shoppers are turned away while exports keep their share.

hints: Not all 14,000 requests are worth the same.
Shedding is cheapest before a request consumes any capacity.
Classify at the edge and reject the class you can most afford to lose.

incidents.title: Fixed rate limit lets a slow database melt the API
incidents.brief: Parcelly's gateway admits a fixed 8,000 req/s. When a Postgres vacuum raises query time from 5 ms to 40 ms, the same 8,000 req/s means 320 in-flight requests instead of 40, and p95 hits 9 s.
incidents.constraint: Database latency swings every hour; no single fixed limit suits both 5 ms and 40 ms.
incidents.question: What limit adapts to how fast the backend is actually draining?

choices.label: Adaptive concurrency limit driven by measured latency

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Tracks real capacity; throughput drops during slow periods and the limiter needs tuning.

choices.resultBody: The gateway compares live latency to its no-load baseline and cuts the concurrency cap multiplicatively when it rises, growing it additively when it falls; in-flight settles near 60, excess gets fast 503s, and p95 drops to 150 ms. Cost: throughput falls to ~1,500 req/s while vacuum runs, and the limiter needs tuning to avoid oscillation.

choices.label: Lower the fixed rate limit to 4,000 req/s
choices.resultBody: At 40 ms, 4,000 req/s is still 160 in flight and p95 stays near 4 s; once the vacuum ends, the limit rejects half the traffic a 5 ms database could have served.

choices.label: Retry timed-out requests twice with exponential backoff
choices.resultBody: Each timeout now costs up to three attempts, pushing effective load toward 14,000 req/s; in-flight passes 500 and API pods start OOM-restarting.

hints: The request rate didn't change; something else multiplied the in-flight work.
In-flight = rate x latency, and latency is the variable here.
Let the limit move with a latency signal instead of a constant.
